title: Chapter 3 — Designing Good Data Architecture: Key Terms

questions.question: How does the book define data architecture?
options: The design of systems to support change in the enterprise, achieved by flexible and reversible decisions reached through careful evaluation of trade-offs.
The design of systems to support the evolving data needs of an enterprise, achieved by flexible and reversible decisions reached through a careful evaluation of trade-offs.
A description of the structure and interaction of the enterprise's major types and sources of data, logical data assets, physical data assets, and data management resources.
An organizational model that aligns strategy, operations, and technology to create a roadmap for success.
questions.explanation: The book defines data architecture as 'the design of systems to support the evolving data needs of an enterprise, achieved by flexible and reversible decisions reached through a careful evaluation of trade-offs.'

questions.question: How does the book define enterprise architecture?
options: The design of systems to support change in the enterprise, achieved by flexible and reversible decisions reached through careful evaluation of trade-offs.
A discipline for proactively leading enterprise responses to disruptive forces by identifying and analyzing the execution of change toward desired business vision and outcomes.
The design of systems to support the evolving data needs of an enterprise, achieved by flexible and reversible decisions reached through a careful evaluation of trade-offs.
A description of the structure and interaction of the enterprise's major types and sources of data.
questions.explanation: The book's definition of enterprise architecture is 'the design of systems to support change in the enterprise, achieved by flexible and reversible decisions reached through careful evaluation of trade-offs.'

questions.question: What does operational architecture describe?
options: Operational architecture describes what needs to be done, encompassing the functional requirements related to people, processes, and technology.
Operational architecture details how data is ingested, stored, transformed, and served along the data engineering lifecycle.
Operational architecture is the design of systems to support the evolving data needs of an enterprise.
Operational architecture defines the physical network topology and hardware specifications of a system.
questions.explanation: The book says operational architecture encompasses the functional requirements of what needs to happen related to people, processes, and technology; it describes what needs to be done.

questions.question: What does technical architecture describe?
options: Technical architecture describes what needs to be done, encompassing the functional requirements related to people, processes, and technology.
Technical architecture is the design of systems to support change in the enterprise.
Technical architecture defines the business processes that the data serves.
Technical architecture outlines how data is ingested, stored, transformed, and served along the data engineering lifecycle, detailing how it will happen.
questions.explanation: The book says technical architecture outlines how data is ingested, stored, transformed, and served along the data engineering lifecycle; it details how something will happen, while operational architecture describes what needs to be done.

questions.question: What is a 'two-way door' in the context of Amazon's decision-making?
options: A decision that is almost impossible to reverse, such as selling a major business unit.
A reversible decision: you walk through the door and proceed if you like what you see, or step back through if you don't.
A decision that requires a five-year planning cycle before it can be executed.
A decision that must be approved by every team in the organization.
questions.explanation: Jeff Bezos describes a two-way door as an easily reversible decision: you walk through and proceed if you like what you see or step back through if you don't. The book urges aiming for two-way doors whenever possible.

questions.question: What characterizes 'good' data architecture, according to the book?
options: Good data architecture serves business requirements with a common, widely reusable set of building blocks while maintaining flexibility and making appropriate trade-offs.
Good data architecture uses the newest, most cutting-edge technologies available for every component.
Good data architecture is authoritarian and crams one-size-fits-all decisions into a big ball of mud.
Good data architecture is tightly coupled, rigid, and overly centralized.
questions.explanation: The book says good data architecture serves business requirements with a common, widely reusable set of building blocks while maintaining flexibility and making appropriate trade-offs; bad architecture is rigid, tightly coupled, and one-size-fits-all.

questions.question: What is a 'common component' in the context of good data architecture?
options: A proprietary database chosen by architects and forced on every team in the organization.
A specialized tool built specifically for one team's domain-specific problem.
A component that is tightly coupled to a single team's stack and cannot be shared.
Anything with broad applicability within an organization, such as object storage, version-control systems, observability, monitoring and orchestration systems, and processing engines.
questions.explanation: The book says common components can be anything that has broad applicability within an organization, including object storage, version-control systems, observability, monitoring and orchestration systems, and processing engines.

questions.question: What is availability, in the context of designing for failure?
options: The system's probability of meeting defined standards in performing its intended function during a specified interval.
The percentage of time an IT service or component is in an operable state.
The maximum acceptable time for a service or system outage.
The maximum acceptable data loss during an outage.
questions.explanation: The book defines availability as the percentage of time an IT service or component is in an operable state.

questions.question: What is reliability, in the context of designing for failure?
options: The percentage of time an IT service or component is in an operable state.
The maximum acceptable data loss during an outage.
The maximum acceptable time for a service or system outage.
The system's probability of meeting defined standards in performing its intended function during a specified interval.
questions.explanation: The book defines reliability as the system's probability of meeting defined standards in performing its intended function during a specified interval.

questions.question: What is the recovery time objective (RTO)?
options: The maximum acceptable time for a service or system outage, generally set by determining the business impact of an outage.
The maximum acceptable data loss during an outage.
The percentage of time an IT service or component is in an operable state.
The system's probability of meeting defined standards in performing its intended function.
questions.explanation: The book defines the recovery time objective (RTO) as the maximum acceptable time for a service or system outage, generally set by determining the business impact of the outage.

questions.question: What is the recovery point objective (RPO)?
options: The maximum acceptable time for a service or system outage.
The percentage of time an IT service or component is in an operable state.
The system's probability of meeting defined standards in performing its intended function.
The maximum acceptable data loss during an outage, representing the acceptable state after recovery.
questions.explanation: The book defines the recovery point objective (RPO) as the maximum acceptable data loss, the acceptable state after recovery.

questions.question: What is scalability, as defined for data systems?
options: The ability of a scalable system to scale dynamically, automatically scaling up and down based on the current workload.
The system's probability of meeting defined standards in performing its intended function during a specified interval.
The ability to increase the capacity of a system to improve performance and handle the demand.
The maximum acceptable data loss during an outage.
questions.explanation: The book defines scalability as allowing us to increase the capacity of a system to improve performance and handle the demand, such as handling a high rate of queries or a huge data set.

questions.question: What is elasticity in the context of scalable systems?
options: The ability to increase the capacity of a system to improve performance and handle the demand.
The maximum acceptable time for a service or system outage.
The percentage of time an IT service or component is in an operable state.
The ability of a scalable system to scale dynamically; a highly elastic system automatically scales up and down based on the current workload.
questions.explanation: The book defines elasticity as the ability of a scalable system to scale dynamically; a highly elastic system can automatically scale up and down based on the current workload.

questions.question: What does it mean for a system to 'scale to zero'?
options: The system shuts down completely when not in use, as many serverless systems can do automatically.
The system scales vertically by adding CPU, disk, memory, and I/O to a single machine.
The system has no ability to scale and must run at a fixed capacity.
The system reduces data retention to zero to cut storage costs.
questions.explanation: The book says some scalable systems can scale to zero: they shut down completely when not in use, and many serverless systems (e.g., serverless functions and serverless OLAP databases) do this automatically.

questions.question: What is FinOps?
options: An evolving cloud financial management discipline and cultural practice that helps engineering, finance, technology, and business teams collaborate on data-driven spending decisions.
A performance engineering approach that maximizes performance for data processes on a fixed set of resources.
A security model that divides responsibility between the cloud provider and the user.
A command-and-control budgeting process where finance teams dictate all technology spending.
questions.explanation: The FinOps Foundation defines FinOps as an evolving cloud financial management discipline and cultural practice that enables organizations to get maximum business value by helping teams collaborate on data-driven spending decisions.

questions.question: What does the shared responsibility model state?
options: The cloud provider is solely responsible for securing everything in the cloud.
The cloud user is solely responsible for securing everything in the cloud.
Security is handled by a hardened network perimeter with trusted things inside.
Security is divided into the security of the cloud (the provider's responsibility) and security in the cloud (the user's responsibility).
questions.explanation: The book says Amazon emphasizes the shared responsibility model, which divides security into the security of the cloud and security in the cloud; providers secure their services, but users are responsible for their applications and data.

questions.question: What is zero-trust security?
options: A security model that places faith in a hardened network perimeter, with trusted things inside and untrusted things outside.
A security model that does not rely on a hardened perimeter, recognizing that external threats effectively become internal threats and that all data engineers are security engineers.
A security model where all assets are isolated from the outside world with no external connectivity.
A security model in which the cloud provider manages all permissions for every user.
questions.explanation: The book contrasts zero-trust security with the traditional hard-perimeter model; in a cloud-native environment the notion of a hardened perimeter erodes, and all data engineers should consider themselves security engineers.

questions.question: What is a domain, as defined in this chapter?
options: A set of functionality whose goal is to accomplish a task.
A single machine or server in a distributed system.
The real-world subject area for which you're architecting—a sphere of knowledge, influence, or activity that the user's program is applied to.
A central data hub used for reporting and analysis.
questions.explanation: The book cites Eric Evans's definition: 'A domain is a sphere of knowledge, influence, or activity,' and adds that a domain is the real-world subject area for which you're architecting.

questions.question: What is a service, as defined in this chapter?
options: A set of functionality whose goal is to accomplish a task.
The real-world subject area for which you're architecting.
A sphere of knowledge, influence, or activity.
A centralized data repository that stores all of an organization's data.
questions.explanation: The book defines a service as a set of functionality whose goal is to accomplish a task; for example, a sales order-processing service's only job is to process orders.

questions.question: What is tight coupling?
options: Decentralized domains and services that do not have strict dependence on each other.
An architecture where teams require little communication to get work done.
A pattern of extremely centralized dependencies and workflows in which every part of a domain and service is vitally dependent on every other domain and service.
A pattern in which components are updated separately as changes and improvements are made.
questions.explanation: The book says on one end of the spectrum you can choose extremely centralized dependencies and workflows, where every part of a domain and service is vitally dependent on every other; this pattern is known as tightly coupled.

questions.question: What is loose coupling?
options: Extremely centralized dependencies and workflows where every part is vitally dependent on every other part.
Decentralized domains and services that do not have strict dependence on each other, so teams can test, deploy, and change systems without dependencies on other teams.
A single codebase running on a single machine that provides both application logic and user interface.
An architecture where the database and application reside on a single server.
questions.explanation: The book describes loose coupling as decentralized domains and services that do not have strict dependence on each other; when architecture and teams are loosely coupled, teams require little communication to get work done.

questions.question: What is a single-tier architecture?
options: An architecture where the database and application are tightly coupled, residing on a single server, so that if the server, database, or application fails, the entire architecture fails.
An architecture composed of separate layers: data, application logic, and presentation.
An architecture made up of separate, decentralized, and loosely coupled services.
An architecture where each node handles a single request and does not share resources with other nodes.
questions.explanation: The book says in a single-tier architecture the database and application are tightly coupled on a single server; while good for prototyping, it is not advised for production because of failure risks.

questions.question: What is a three-tier architecture?
options: An architecture where the database and application are tightly coupled on a single server.
An architecture made up of separate, decentralized, and loosely coupled services.
An architecture where a single node handles each request and nodes do not share memory, disk, or CPU.
A widely used client-server design consisting of data, application logic, and presentation tiers, each isolated from the other to allow separation of concerns.
questions.explanation: The book describes a common multitier architecture as the three-tier architecture, a widely used client-server design consisting of data, application logic, and presentation tiers, each isolated from the other for separation of concerns.

questions.question: What is a monolith, in its most extreme version?
options: A single codebase running on a single machine that provides both the application logic and user interface.
A system broken into many small components that interface through abstraction layers such as APIs.
A system where each service has a specific function and is decoupled from other services.
A system that is decentralized with no strict dependence between domains.
questions.explanation: The book says the general notion of a monolith includes as much as possible under one roof; in its most extreme version, it consists of a single codebase running on a single machine providing both application logic and user interface.

questions.question: What is technical coupling within a monolith?
options: Coupling that refers to the way domains are coupled together.
Coupling that refers to architectural tiers.
Coupling that refers to how teams communicate with one another.
Coupling that refers to the sharing of database schemas between departments.
questions.explanation: The book says coupling within monoliths can be viewed in two ways: technical coupling refers to architectural tiers, while domain coupling refers to the way domains are coupled together.

questions.question: What is domain coupling?
options: Coupling that refers to architectural tiers.
Coupling between the database and the application layer.
Coupling that refers to the way domains are coupled together.
Coupling between worker nodes in a distributed system.
questions.explanation: The book says domain coupling refers to the way domains are coupled together, as distinct from technical coupling, which refers to architectural tiers.

questions.question: What is a microservices architecture?
options: A single codebase running on a single machine that provides both application logic and user interface.
An architecture where the database and application are tightly coupled on a single server.
An architecture with data, application logic, and presentation tiers.
An architecture made up of separate, decentralized, and loosely coupled services, each with a specific function, so that if one service goes down it won't affect the others.
questions.explanation: The book says microservices architecture comprises separate, decentralized, and loosely coupled services, each with a specific function; if one service temporarily goes down, it won't affect other services' ability to function.

questions.question: What is multitenancy, as discussed in this chapter?
options: Giving each customer a dedicated physical server to guarantee isolation.
Allowing only a single team to access a given system.
Sharing systems across multiple teams, organizations, and customers, at various grains, requiring consideration of performance isolation and data security.
Merging all tenants' data into a single table with no isolation mechanisms.
questions.explanation: The book says engineers make decisions about sharing systems across multiple teams, organizations, and customers; all cloud services are multitenant at various grains, with factors of performance (noisy neighbor) and security (data isolation) to consider.

questions.question: What is an event-driven architecture?
options: An architecture that embraces the event-driven workflow and uses events to communicate across services, distributing the state of an event across multiple services.
An architecture where services communicate by directly reading each other's data stores.
An architecture with a single codebase providing both application logic and user interface.
An architecture where batch and streaming systems operate independently in separate layers.
questions.explanation: The book says an event-driven architecture embraces the event-driven workflow and uses it to communicate across services; its advantage is that it distributes the state of an event across multiple services, and any time you have loosely coupled services this is a candidate for it.

questions.question: What is a brownfield project?
options: A project that allows you to pioneer a fresh start, unconstrained by the history or legacy of a prior architecture.
A project that involves refactoring and reorganizing an existing architecture and is constrained by the choices of the present and past.
A project that replaces a legacy system with a direct all-at-once rewrite.
A project that uses only the newest and coolest tools available.
questions.explanation: The book says brownfield projects often involve refactoring and reorganizing an existing architecture and are constrained by the choices of the present and past, requiring a thorough understanding of the legacy architecture.

questions.question: What is a greenfield project?
options: A project that is constrained by the choices of the present and past of an existing architecture.
A project that slowly and incrementally replaces a legacy architecture's components.
A project that allows you to pioneer a fresh start, unconstrained by the history or legacy of a prior architecture.
A project that involves a big-bang overhaul of the old architecture all at once.
questions.explanation: The book says a greenfield project allows you to pioneer a fresh start, unconstrained by the history or legacy of a prior architecture, and tends to be easier than a brownfield project.

questions.question: What is the strangler pattern?
options: An all-at-once, big-bang overhaul of a legacy architecture, often figuring out deprecation as you go.
A pattern in which new systems slowly and incrementally replace a legacy architecture's components, eventually completely replacing it.
A greenfield approach where you start with a clean slate and the newest tools.
A pattern of forcing every team to use one proprietary technology.
questions.explanation: The book describes the strangler pattern as an alternative to a direct rewrite: new systems slowly and incrementally replace a legacy architecture's components, eventually replacing the legacy architecture completely.

questions.question: What is a data warehouse, as described in this chapter?
options: A central data hub used for reporting and analysis, in which data is typically highly formatted and structured for analytics use cases.
A central repository that stores all data, structured and unstructured, without imposing tight structural limitations.
A more refined subset of a warehouse focused on a single department or line of business.
A system that incorporates warehouse controls while housing data in object storage and supporting ACID transactions.
questions.explanation: The book says a data warehouse is a central data hub used for reporting and analysis, typically containing data highly formatted and structured for analytics; it cites Inmon's definition of it as subject-oriented, integrated, nonvolatile, and time-variant.

questions.question: What does ETL stand for, and what does it describe?
options: Extract, transform, load: a process that pulls data from source systems, cleans and standardizes it while imposing business logic, then loads it into the data warehouse target database.
Extract, load, transform: data moved directly into the warehouse with transformations handled inside the warehouse.
Evaluate, transfer, and log: a process for monitoring data pipelines.
Export, transform, and link: a process for sharing data between domains.
questions.explanation: The book describes ETL as having an extract phase that pulls data from source systems, a transformation phase that cleans and standardizes data, and a load phase that pushes data into the data warehouse target database system.

questions.question: What is ELT?
options: Extract, transform, load, where transformations are performed in an external processing system before loading.
Evaluate, load, and test: a quality-assurance process for data pipelines.
Export, load, and translate: a process for moving data between data lakes.
Extract, load, transform: data is moved more or less directly into a staging area in the data warehouse, and transformations are handled directly in the warehouse to leverage its computational power.
questions.explanation: The book says with the ELT data warehouse architecture, data is moved more or less directly from production systems into a staging area in the warehouse, and transformations are handled directly in the warehouse rather than in an external system.

questions.question: What is MPP in the context of data warehouse architecture?
options: Massively parallel processing systems, which are optimized to scan massive amounts of data in parallel and allow high-performance aggregation and statistical calculations.
A single-server system scaled vertically by increasing CPU, disk, and memory.
A message queue used for streaming data ingestion.
An object storage system used to house unstructured data.
questions.explanation: The book says MPPs (first popularized in the 1980s) support SQL semantics but are optimized to scan massive amounts of data in parallel, allowing high-performance aggregation and statistical calculations.

questions.question: What is a cloud data warehouse?
options: A data warehouse that requires sizing an MPP system for several years and signing a multimillion-dollar contract to procure it.
A repository that dumps all structured and unstructured data without structural limitations.
A data warehouse delivered as a pay-as-you-go cloud service, often separating compute from storage so users can spin up computing power on demand.
A data mart that serves a single department's analytics needs.
questions.explanation: The book says cloud data warehouses represent a significant evolution of the on-premises warehouse; Amazon Redshift kicked off the revolution, and BigQuery and Snowflake popularized separating compute from storage with pay-as-you-go scalability.

questions.question: What is a data mart?
options: A central data hub used for reporting and analysis for the entire organization.
A repository that stores all data, structured and unstructured, without imposing tight structural limitations.
A more refined subset of a warehouse designed to serve analytics and reporting, focused on a single suborganization, department, or line of business.
A system that incorporates warehouse controls while housing data in object storage.
questions.explanation: The book says a data mart is a more refined subset of a warehouse designed to serve analytics and reporting, focused on a single suborganization, department, or line of business, in contrast to the full warehouse that serves the broader organization.

questions.question: What is a data lake?
options: A central repository that stores all of your data, structured and unstructured, without imposing tight structural limitations.
A central data hub used for reporting and analysis, with data highly formatted and structured for analytics.
A refined subset of a warehouse focused on a single department.
A system that combines warehouse data management controls with object storage.
questions.explanation: The book describes the data lake as an architecture that instead of imposing tight structural limitations on data simply dumps all data, structured and unstructured, into a central location.

questions.question: What is a data lakehouse?
options: The first-generation data lake, which started with HDFS and was essentially write-only.
A data lake that has become a dumping ground of unmanageable data.
A data warehouse that uses ETL and centralized organizational structures.

An architecture that incorporates the controls, data management, and data structures of a data warehouse while still housing data in object storage and supporting a variety of query and transformation engines, including ACID transactions.
questions.explanation: The book says Databricks introduced the data lakehouse, which incorporates warehouse controls, data management, and data structures while housing data in object storage; notably it supports ACID transactions, a big departure from the original data lake.

questions.question: What is the modern data stack?
options: An expensive, monolithic toolset with releases and roadmaps largely hidden from users.
A stack that relies on custom-built proprietary technologies with unclear pricing.
A trendy analytics architecture that uses cloud-based, plug-and-play, easy-to-use, off-the-shelf components to create a modular and cost-effective data architecture.
A data warehouse architecture based on ETL pipelines and data marts.
questions.explanation: The book says the main objective of the modern data stack is to use cloud-based, plug-and-play, easy-to-use, off-the-shelf components to create a modular and cost-effective data architecture, reducing complexity and increasing modularization.

questions.question: What is the Lambda architecture?
options: An architecture that uses a stream-processing platform as the backbone for all data handling, covering ingestion, storage, and serving.
An architecture with independent batch, streaming (speed), and serving layers, where the source system is ideally immutable and append-only, sending data to both stream and batch destinations.
An architecture that views all data as events aggregated over windows.
An architecture where data is processed only in batch using a data warehouse.
questions.explanation: The book says in a Lambda architecture you have systems operating independently of each other—batch, streaming, and serving; the source system is ideally immutable and append-only, sending data to a speed layer and a batch layer, with a serving layer aggregating results.

questions.question: What is the Kappa architecture?
options: An architecture with separate batch, speed, and serving layers that run independently.
An architecture that keeps batch and streaming on different codebases that are reconciled later.

An architecture, proposed by Jay Kreps, that uses a stream-processing platform as the backbone for all data handling—ingestion, storage, and serving—so real-time and batch processing apply seamlessly to the same data.
An architecture based on a centralized monolithic data warehouse.
questions.explanation: The book says Jay Kreps proposed the Kappa architecture as a response to Lambda's shortcomings: why not use a stream-processing platform as the backbone for all data handling, reading the live event stream directly and replaying large chunks for batch processing.

questions.question: What is the core idea of the Dataflow model?
options: To maintain separate code paths for batch and streaming so each can be optimized independently.
To route all data through a centralized data warehouse before it is served.
To treat all data as immutable files stored in a distributed file system.

To view all data as events, with aggregation performed over various types of windows; real-time streams are unbounded data, batches are bounded event streams, and real-time and batch processing happen in the same system with nearly identical code.
questions.explanation: The book says the core idea of the Dataflow model is to view all data as events, aggregating over windows; ongoing real-time event streams are unbounded data, batches are simply bounded event streams, and processing happens in the same system with nearly identical code.

questions.question: What is the data mesh?
options: A centralized data architecture in which a single team gathers data from all domains and reconciles it for consumption across the organization.
A monolithic data lake owned centrally by a central data platform team.

A recent response to sprawling monolithic data platforms that inverts the challenges of centralized data architecture by applying domain-driven design concepts to data, with domain-oriented decentralized data ownership and data as a product.
A data warehouse architecture organized around ETL and data marts.
questions.explanation: The book says the data mesh is a recent response to sprawling monolithic data platforms and 'the great divide of data,' applying domain-driven design concepts to data architecture; Dehghani's four components include domain-oriented decentralized data ownership, data as a product, self-serve data infrastructure as a platform, and federated computational governance.
